source_text: Oratio in illud: Dominus creavit me initium viarum suarum (fragmenta) Ο ΛΟΓΟΣ Ο ΕΙΣ ΤΟ· ΚΥΡΙΟΣ ΕΚΤΙΣΕ ΜΕ ΑΡΧΗΝ Ο∆ΩΝ ΑΥΤΟΥ 18 Εἰ μὲν οὖν ἀρχὴν τῆς γεννήσεως εἴληφεν ὁ Λόγος, ἀφ' οὗ διὰ τῆς μητρῴας διοδεύσας γαστρὸς τὰς σωματικὰς ἐφόρεσεν ἁρμονίας, συνέστηκεν ὅτι γέγονεν ἐκ γυναικός. Εἰ δὲ Λόγος καὶ Θεὸς ἦν ἀνέκαθεν παρὰ τῷ Πατρὶ καὶ τὰ σύμπαντα δι' αὐτοῦ γεγενῆσθαί φαμεν, οὐκ ἄρα γέγονεν ἐκ γυναικὸς ὁ ὢν, καὶ τοῖς γεννητοῖς ἅπασιν αἴτιος ὤν· ἀλλ' ἔστι τὴν φύσιν Θεὸς αὐτάρκης, ἄπειρος, ἀπερινόητος· ἐκ γυναικὸς δὲ γέγονεν ἄνθρωπος, ὁ ἐν τῇ παρθενικῇ μήτρᾳ Πνεύματι παγεὶς ἁγίῳ. 19 Ναὸς γὰρ κυρίως ὁ καθαρὸς καὶ ἄχραντος, ἡ κατὰ τὸν ἄνθρωπόν ἐστι περὶ τὸν Λόγον σκηνὴ, ἔνθα προφανῶς σκηνώσας ᾤκησεν ὁ Θεός. Καὶ ταῦτα οὐκ ἐκ τῶν εἰκότων φαμέν· τούτου γὰρ ὁ φύσει τοῦ Θεοῦ Υἱὸς, τὴν λύσι καὶ ἀνάστασιν προαγορεύων τοῦ νεὼ, ἀναμφιβόλως ἡμᾶς διδάσκων ἐφοδιάζει, τοῖς μιαιφόνοις φάσκων Ἰουδαίοις· λύσατε τὸν ναὸν τοῦτον, καὶ ἐν τρισὶν ἡμέραις ἐγερῶ αὐτόν. 20 Ὁπηνίκα οὖν τὸν ἄνθρωπον ναουργήσας ἐφόρεσεν ὁ Λόγος, σώματι μὲν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ἐπιφοιτῶν, παντοδαπὰς ἀοράτως θαυματουργίας ἐπεδείκνυτο, τοὺς δὲ ἀποστόλους κήρυκας τῆς ἀϊδίου βασιλείας ἐξέπεμπε. 21 Οὐ γὰρ εἶπεν ὁ Παῦλος συμμόρφους τοῦ Υἱοῦ τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἀλλὰ συμμόρφους τῆς εἰκόνος τοῦ Υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ, ἄλλο μέν τι δεικνύων τὸν Υἱὸν εἶναι, ἄλλο δὲ τὴν εἰκόνα αὐτοῦ. Ὁ μὲν γὰρ Υἱὸς, τὰ θεῖα τῆς πατρῴας ἀρετῆς γνωρίσματα φέρων, εἰκών ἐστι τοῦ Παρτός· ἐπειδὴ καὶ ὅμοιοι ἐξ ὁμοίων γεννώμενοι, εἰκόνες οἱ τικτόμενοι φαίνονται τῶν γεννητόρων ἀληθεῖς. Ὁ δὲ ἄνθρωπος ὃν ἐφόρεσεν, εἰκών ἐστι τοῦ Υἱοῦ, τοῦ καὶ ἐξ ἀνομοίων κηρογραφεῖσθαι χρωμάτων εἰκόνας· καὶ τὰς μὲν εἶναι θέσει χειροτεύκτους, τὰς δὲ φύσει καὶ ὁμοιότητι γεγενημένας. Ἄλλως τε καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ τῆς ἀληθείας τοῦθ' ὑπαγορεύει θεσμός. Οὐ γὰρ τὸ ἀσώματον τῆς Σοφίας Πνεῦμα σύμμορφον τοῖς σωματικοῖς ἀνθρώποις ἐστίν, ἀλλ' ὁ τῷ Πνεύματι σωματοποιηθεὶς ἄνθρωπος χαρακτὴρ, ὁ τοῖς· ἄλλοις ἅπασι ἰσάριθμα μέλη φορῶν, καὶ τὴν ὁμοίαν ἑκάστοις περιβεβλημένος ἰδέαν. 22 Ὅτι δὲ τὸ σῶμα λέγει σύμμορφον τοῖς ἀνθρωπίνοις εἶναι, σαφέστερον ἡμᾶς διδάσκει Φιλιππησίοις ἐπιστέλλων· Ἡμῶν τὸ πολίτευμα, φησίν, ἐν οὐρανοῖς ὑπάρχει, ἐξ οὗ καὶ σωτῆρα ἀπεκδεχόμεθα Κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν, ὃς μετασχηματίσει τὸ σῶμα τῆς ταπεινώσεως ἡμῶν, εἰς τὸ γενέσθαι αὐτὸ σύμμορφον τῷ σώματι τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ. Εἰ δὲ τὸ ταπεινὸν μετασχηματίζων τῶν ἀνθρώπων σῶμα, σύμμορφον τῷ ἰδίῳ σώματι κατασκευάζει, ἕωλος πανταχόθεν ἀποδέδεικται ἡ τῶν ἐναντίων συκοφαντία.
thought_title: The Word is God from eternity; the man born of woman is his temple
orientation: Eustathius opens his treatise by distinguishing the eternal divine Word from the man whom the Word fashioned and wore, arguing that only the man was born of a woman.
pass_a_gloss: If then the Word received a beginning of generation, from which time he passed through the maternal womb and wore the bodily harmonies, it is established that he came to be from a woman. But if he was Word and God from the beginning with the Father, and we say that all things came to be through him, then the one who is, and who is cause of all generated things, did not come to be from a woman; but he is by nature God, self-sufficient, boundless, incomprehensible; but from a woman came to be a man, the one formed in the virginal womb by the Holy Spirit. For properly the temple is the pure and undefiled tent around the Word according to the man, where God clearly dwelt after pitching his tent. And these things we say not from probabilities; for the Son by nature of God, foretelling the destruction and resurrection of the temple, equips us by teaching unambiguously, saying to the murderous Jews: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it. When therefore the Word, having built the man as a temple, wore him, appearing to humans in body, he displayed all kinds of wonders invisibly, and sent out the apostles as heralds of the eternal kingdom. For Paul did not say conformed to the Son of God, but conformed to the image of his Son, showing that the Son is one thing, and his image another. For the Son, bearing the divine marks of the Father's excellence, is the image of the Father; since also like offspring born from like parents, the offspring appear as true images of their begetters. But the man whom he wore is the image of the Son, who also fashions images from unlike colors; and some are handmade by placement, but others have come to be by nature and likeness. Besides, the very law of truth dictates this. For the incorporeal Spirit of Wisdom is not conformed to bodily humans, but the man given body by the Spirit is the imprint, wearing members equal in number to all others, and clothed in the same form as each. And that he says the body is conformed to human bodies, he teaches us more clearly when writing to the Philippians: Our citizenship, he says, exists in heaven, from which also we await a savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humiliation, so that it may become conformed to the body of his glory. But if by transforming the humble body of humans he makes it conformed to his own body, the slander of the opponents has been shown stale from every side.

pass_b_english: If the Word received a beginning of generation from the time when he passed through his mother's womb and wore the bodily frame, then it follows that he came from a woman. But if the Word was God from the beginning with the Father, and we say that all things were made through him, then the one who exists and is the cause of all generated things did not come from a woman. Rather, he is by nature self-sufficient God, boundless, incomprehensible. What came from a woman is the man, the one formed in the virginal womb by the Holy Spirit.

For the pure and undefiled temple, properly speaking, is the tent around the Word according to the man, where God visibly pitched his tent and dwelt. And we do not say this from mere likelihood. The natural Son of God, foretelling the destruction and resurrection of the temple, equips us by teaching beyond doubt when he says to the murderous Jews, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" (John 2:19).

So when the Word had built the man as a temple and wore him, he visited human beings in a body and displayed all kinds of wonders invisibly, and he sent out the apostles as heralds of the eternal kingdom.

For Paul did not say that we are conformed to the Son of God, but conformed to the image of his Son, showing that the Son is one thing and his image another. The Son, bearing the divine marks of the Father's excellence, is the image of the Father; for when like offspring are born from like parents, the children appear as true images of their begetters. But the man whom he wore is the image of the Son, as images are painted from unlike colors: some are handmade by art, while others come into being by nature and likeness. Besides, the very law of truth dictates this. For the incorporeal Spirit of Wisdom is not conformed to bodily human beings; rather, the man given body by the Spirit is the imprint, bearing members equal in number to all other human beings and clothed in the same form as each of them.

That he means the body is conformed to human bodies, he teaches us more clearly when writing to the Philippians: "Our citizenship is in heaven, from which we also await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory" (Philippians 3:20-21). If he transforms the lowly body of human beings and makes it conformed to his own body, then the slander of the opponents has been shown to be stale on every side.

problems.why: ἀοράτως is adverb 'invisibly' or 'unseen,' modifying the manner of displaying, not 'invisible wonders.' The miracles were visible; they were performed invisibly (i.e., by hidden/divine power). 'Invisible wonders' suggests the wonders themselves could not be seen, which is wrong.
θέσει means 'by position/appointment/convention' (opposed to φύσει 'by nature'), not 'by design.' This is a philosophical contrast between conventional/nominal and natural. 'By design' is wrong.
problems.ruling: θέσει contrasts φύσει as 'by convention/position,' not 'by design'; philosophical distinction lost.

problems.why: ἕωλος means 'stale, day-old, worn-out,' but πανταχόθεν ἀποδέδεικται means 'has been shown/refuted from every side.' The English 'stale from every side' is nonsensical — 'stale' modifies the slander, but 'from every side' goes with the demonstration. It should be 'shown to be stale from every side' or 'refuted on every side as stale.'
problems.fix: shown to be stale on every side
problems.ruling: ἕωλος πανταχόθεν ἀποδέδεικται = 'shown stale from every side'; English 'stale from every side' detaches πανταχόθεν from ἀποδέδεικται, misleading.

fixed: The phrase 'the man, the one formed in the virginal womb by the Holy Spirit' accurately renders the source's 'ἐκ γυναικὸς δὲ γέγονεν ἄνθρωπος, ὁ ἐν τῇ παρθενικῇ μήτρᾳ Πνεύματι παγεὶς ἁγίῳ'; the English already uses 'the man' consistently for ἄνθρωπος, so no edit is needed.

The source uses ναός (temple) and σκηνή (tent) as distinct but related metaphors; the English preserves both, and the phrase 'the tent around the Word according to the man' is a faithful rendering of 'ἡ κατὰ τὸν ἄνθρωπόν ἐστι περὶ τὸν Λόγον σκηνὴ', so no edit is needed.

The two-level image scheme is already clear in the English: the Son is the image of the Father, and the man is the image of the Son; the source's 'εἰκών' is consistently rendered as 'image', so no edit is needed.

The source's 'τοῦ καὶ ἐξ ἀνομοίων κηρογραφεῖσθαι χρωμάτων εἰκόνας' refers to the Son as the one who fashions images from unlike colors; the English 'as images of him are painted from unlike colors' misreads the grammar, so I have corrected it to 'as images are painted from unlike colors' to match the source's general statement about image-making.

The source's 'ὁ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἅπασι ἰσάριθμα μέλη φορῶν' means 'bearing members equal in number to all the others', i.e., all other human beings; the English 'all the rest' is ambiguous, so I have clarified it to 'all other human beings'.

The source's 'ἡ κατὰ τὸν ἄνθρωπόν ἐστι περὶ τὸν Λόγον σκηνὴ' is accurately rendered as 'the tent around the Word according to the man'; the English preserves the source's distinction between ναός and σκηνή, so no edit is needed.

The source's 'τὸ ἀσώματον τῆς Σοφίας Πνεῦμα' is accurately rendered as 'the incorporeal Spirit of Wisdom'; the English consistently uses 'Spirit' for Πνεῦμα and 'Wisdom' for Σοφία, so no edit is needed.

The source's 'Ὁ δὲ ἄνθρωπος ὃν ἐφόρεσεν, εἰκών ἐστι τοῦ Υἱοῦ' is accurately rendered as 'the man whom he wore is the image of the Son'; the English consistently uses 'image' for εἰκών, so no edit is needed.
